name: Ethiopian Empire (Menelik II)

areaKm2.note: Statesman's Year-Book 1913: 432,432 sq mi = 1.12 million km2 (high), close to the world_1914 Abyssinia polygon (about 1.14 million km2 on the sphere) used as the border. Kaffa (1897), Beni Shangul (1898) and the southern and Ogaden marches were taken or fixed after Adwa, so 1896 lies below that (mid, low: reduction by educated guess). The 1880/1900 basemaps draw only the northern highlands ("Ethiopia", about 277,000 km2, without Shewa or Addis Ababa) and are not used.

population.note: Low: estimated 8 million for the 1913 empire (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Statesman%27s_Year-Book_1913/Abyssinia). 12,180,600 for 1900 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_population_in_1900, footnote not checked). High: OWID Ethiopia 1890 = 17.86M, 1900 = 17.72M (Gapminder v7, modern borders, https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population), likely high. Mid 11 million between the contemporary and the list figure. The 1899 Year-Book's 3.5 million covers only the 150,000 sq mi of Abyssinia proper (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Statesman%27s_Year-Book_1899/Abyssinia). No census.

urbanization.note: Statesman's Year-Book 1899: almost no towns over 5,000 (Ankober 7,000, Aksum and Gondar 5,000, Adwa 3,000; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Statesman%27s_Year-Book_1899/Abyssinia); 1913: Addis Ababa 40,000-50,000 and Harar 50,000 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Statesman%27s_Year-Book_1913/Abyssinia). Towns of 5,000+ held about 60,000-150,000 people of 8-11 million.

activePersonnel.note: Army mobilized by Menelik's awaj (call to arms) of September 1895 and assembled at Adwa: 73,000-100,000 (McLachlan 2011 p. 20; Ahmad and Pankhurst 1998 pp. 158-62), over 100,000 in the Petrides and Pankhurst breakdown (via Uhlig); mid just above 100,000 to fit the force split below. High: regular army about 150,000 men drawn from provincial contingents (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Statesman%27s_Year-Book_1899/Abyssinia). Camp followers, about as many again, are not counted.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: provincial troops and territorial levies not marched north, and the unknown number of armed peasants McLachlan notes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Adwa).

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess: gunners of about 42 guns and the imperial household's armourers; muleteers are camp followers and not counted.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess: the awaj called every able-bodied man of the Christian highlands; the 1896 army of 73,000-150,000 was about 1% of 8-11 million people, and the wider levy pool is set at 2-4%, near the Mughal 3% armed-peasantry analogy used for South Asia.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Riflemen of the regional contingents (McLachlan 2011 p. 42, via the article): Shewa 25,000, Semien 3,000, Gojjam 5,000, Harar 15,000, Tigray 12,000, Wollo 6,000, Gondar 8,000, Lasta 6,000 = 80,000 rifles (high); mid deducts the mounted riflemen counted as cavalry.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5 (era-typical) minus. Evidence: imported breech-loading rifles of mixed patterns, mostly single-shot, against Italian Vetterli and Carcano rifles; ammunition supply uneven.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: experienced warriors of the provincial retinues, good shots, but no formal drill or regimental training.

count.note: About 20,000 spearmen and swordsmen (McLachlan 2011 p. 42, via the article) (mid); high adds part of the armed peasants of unknown number.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25 or below. Evidence: spears, swords and shields in a rifle war.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: retainers and levies with no drill.

count.note: Horses listed by McLachlan 2011 p. 42: Shewa 3,000, Semien 600, Wollo 5,000 = 8,600 (low); Petrides and Pankhurst (via Uhlig): 8,000 cavalry under Menelik and 5,000 Oromo cavalry under Ras Mikael = 13,000 (high). Both via the article.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: small highland horses, lances and some rifles.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Oromo horsemen under Ras Mikael, effective in the pursuit at Adwa.

count.note: Guns listed by McLachlan 2011 p. 42 (via the article): Shewa 32, Semien 4, Tigray 6 = 42. High allows for guns of contingents whose entries list rifles only.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: imported mountain and field guns, comparable with the Italian mountain batteries at Adwa.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: few trained gunners; artillery a small arm of the army.

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Menelik united rival rases, concentrated an army over 1,000 km and let Baratieri attack into prepared positions at Adwa.

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.5, between a feudal host (0.25) and a national army. Evidence: regional contingents under their own rases, held together by the emperor; the army would melt away once local food ran out (Battle of Adwa article).

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.75-1.0. Evidence: defence against invasion; victories at Amba Alagi (December 1895) and Mekelle (January 1896).

weapons.note: Anchor: 6 (1805) to 7 (1905, magazine rifle, QF artillery). Evidence: breech-loading rifles and imported guns, few magazine rifles and machine guns; spears for a fifth of the army.

armor.note: Anchor: 5 (half-armour) to 6 (none). Evidence: hide shields only; no body armour. Set below 6 because shields, not drill and entrenching, were the protection.

ships.note: Anchor: 0. Evidence: landlocked after Italy took Massawa (1885); no navy.

fortification.note: Anchor: 4-5. Evidence: amba hill strongholds and walled Harar; besieged the Italian fort at Mekelle by cutting its water rather than by artillery.

logistics.note: Anchor: 4 (granaries, pack animals). Evidence: army lived off the land with mules and camp followers and had to fight or disperse when local supplies ran out (Battle of Adwa article).

communications.note: Anchor: 5-6. Evidence: runners and mounted couriers; a telegraph line Addis Ababa-Harar existed by 1899 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Statesman%27s_Year-Book_1899/Abyssinia), whether it worked in early 1896 was not checked.

isr.note: Anchor: 5. Evidence: local spies and guides; the Italians marched on Adwa with poor maps and misled by informants.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023: Ethiopia's first value is 1950 = 622 (2011 int$); held back to 1896 on the stagnation assumption, mid about that. High reflects the Sub-Saharan Africa regional average (1870 = 1,286, which SOURCES.md notes overstates the region) scaled down; low near subsistence.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. War-year value (low = peacetime). Soldiers were paid mainly through land grants (gult) and quartering on peasants, so a cash share is not documented.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess: crafts (weaving, smithing) only; all rifles and guns were imported.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Plough agriculture of the highlands, weakened by the Great Famine of 1888-92; a concentrated army exhausted a district within weeks.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the other pre-modern snapshots.

roadKm.note: In 1913 roads were mostly mere tracks with only a few miles of metalled road in and near the capital; in 1896 there were fewer still.

railKm.note: The Jibuti-Harar line was still a project in 1899 (70 of 186 miles surveyed, 12 miles laid, starting from Jibuti); none in Ethiopia in 1896.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess: no coast; imports came through Italian Massawa, French Obock/Jibuti and British Zeila.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. The army foraged where it stood; it marched from Shewa to Tigray (about 800 km) by living off successive districts, not on a supply line.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: mules, donkeys, horses and plough oxen of a highland farming country (about 10% of the population); no count found.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2-1.3: mountainous highlands, amba strongholds and population support; long, exposed supply lines for an invader from the coast. Below the full 1.3 row because the highland climate did not defeat the Italians.

notes: Snapshot = February 1896, Menelik's army concentrated at Adwa before the battle of 1 March. Personnel: the mobilized army (riflemen, spearmen, cavalry, gunners) is activePersonnel; territorial levies and armed peasants not marched north are trainedReserves; camp followers are not counted. Force figures from the Battle of Adwa article (McLachlan 2011 regional breakdown, Petrides and Pankhurst). Population is the weakest value (8 to 17.7 million; no census) and the border (world_1914 Abyssinia) postdates the snapshot by 18 years, so area and population include lands annexed 1897-1900. Economy and logistics are educated guesses except roads and railways. Doctrine archetype-feudal-host: provincial contingents of the rases raised by the emperor's call.
